SimHub is not running as administrator. This is required for reliable force feedback (the USB capture that mirrors the game's FFB can fail without it). Easiest fix: turn on 'Run as administrator' in SimHub's Settings, then restart SimHub.

Your wheel is connected, but FFB pass-through can't find it on the USB bus, so your game's force feedback may feel wrong or be silenced. This is most often fixed by restarting your computer: the capture driver only loads at boot, so a fresh install needs one reboot. The engine's firing pulse through the wheel, rising with RPM.
Set the engine type in Car facts (active car card) for the most accurate pulse.
0 = disabled. Lowers buzzy harmonics on Square/Saw without changing pitch.

What Engine pulse does for electric cars (detected as electric, or set to Electric in Car facts). Most users prefer the muted hum since real EVs aren't silent (many pump synthetic engine sound). Pick Silent if you want true silence on EVs.

Adds a low-frequency oscillation at the engine's cycle rate (RPM/120 Hz) alongside the firing pulse. Sits in the band the wheel actually moves at, so the engine keeps feeling present as the firing pulse rolls off at high RPM.
Extra engine-pulse strength that ramps in above 50% RPM, so high revs stay strong in the wheel instead of fading.
The extra whack the instant a wheel first strikes a hard bump: ruts, edges, drops. 0 = smooth texture only.

Forza-only: drives a second oscillator from the per-tire SurfaceRumble channel. Continuous road feel that's stronger on dirt/grass and lighter on asphalt. Curb thump handles the hit when a wheel first finds a curb.
Multiplier on Forza's SurfaceRumble before driving the oscillator. 1.0 = use as-is. Bump up for more aggressive surface feel.
Cut high frequencies from noise. Lower = smoother rumble, higher = grittier.
Cut sub-audible drift / DC thump from noise. 0 disables.

Feel which axle is slipping: a high scrub texture as the front washes wide, a deep pulse as the rear steps out. The louder axle is the one losing grip. Needs per-tire telemetry (Forza, Assetto Corsa, and Farming Simulator with the TF4ALL Enhanced Telemetry mod).
Volume of the high front scrub voice, under the main gain.
Volume of the deep rear pulse voice, under the main gain.
Center of the front scrub tone (default 200). Lower = smoother rub, higher = sharper hiss. The tone still climbs as the front tires reach the limit.
Center of the rear thump (default 35). Lower = heavier, slower thud. Also the floor for the wheelspin-locked pulse.
Depth of the grip-slip-grip chatter once the front is past the limit. 0 = smooth scrub only.
How close to the grip limit before the voices start speaking. 0.85 = 85% of the limit; lower = earlier warning.
Predicts the slide from how fast grip is being used up, so the warning arrives a fraction before the limit instead of at it.
The rear pulse speeds up and slows down with the spinning wheels themselves, so wheelspin feels like wheels turning rather than a generic buzz.
A single firm whack the instant a wheel first touches a curb, distinct from the rumble that follows. Scales with speed. Needs curb telemetry (Forza games today).
Lower = deeper whack. 30 Hz default keeps it below the gear-shift thud.
A flat-spot pulse while a braking tire is locked, slowing with the car the way a real flat spot would. Needs per-tire telemetry (Forza and Assetto Corsa today).
A mechanical clunk in the wheel when equipment drops into work or lifts back out, the linkage landing and releasing. Lowering lands harder than raising.
How hard lifting OUT of work lands, relative to dropping in. 0 = raising is silent.
A pump whine while the linkage or a fold is actually traveling; the thud then lands when the motion settles. 0 = thud only.
The pump's pitch. Sits above the thud's knock so the two read as one mechanism.
How far the whine spools up from below its pitch as motion starts, and again as it settles. 0 = flat pitch.
How much a fast-moving linkage raises the whine's pitch.
How much slow hydraulic movement quiets the whine: it swells as motion picks up and fades as it eases into the stop. 0 = constant loudness.
A higher second tone inside the whine so it reads as machinery, not a pure hum. 0 = single tone.
Forza Horizon's Data Out telemetry doesn't include ABS pump activity, so this effect will stay silent in FH4/FH5/FH6 regardless of the values you set here.
Per tick (one click per ABS pump)
Feels like the engine being cut at low RPM while the pit limiter is engaged: a steady pulse train you can't miss. Works in most racing sims that have a pit lane.
Tone within each pulse. Lower = deeper thud; higher = brighter.
How fast the pulse opens / closes. 5-10 Hz feels like a real pit limiter cadence.
How much of each pulse is filled with sound. Higher = more sustained; lower = more punctuated.
Peak amplitude while the limiter is engaged.
A quick chirp the moment DRS opens, then a faint sustained tone while the wing stays open. Silent on games that don't expose DRS.
Shape of the brief blip on the rising edge.
Sustained tone (while DRS held open). Set amp to 0 for chirp-only mode.
Shape of the held trail. Independent from the activation chirp so a sharp Square blip can have a softer Sine trail.
Project CARS 2 supplies its native impact magnitude; other games derive it from sudden acceleration spikes above about 5g, well above hard cornering or curbs.
A thud on impact that hits harder the bigger the crash.
Lower = lighter contacts trigger. Raise if light scrapes are too noisy.
Cap on the loudest hit. Safety knob for wrists / wheelbase.
Shape of the impact thud. Square is the punchiest; Sine is softer.
A hard buzz when you enter the redline start: an unmistakable shift cue. If it fires at the wrong RPM, fix the redline start in Car facts.
The buzz is firing at 85% of max RPM because no one has confirmed the real redline start yet (where the tachometer turns red). Set it so the shift cue lands right.
Shift the engage point relative to the car's redline. Negative fires the buzz before the redline (an early shift cue); positive fires it after. 0 = right at the redline.
Tone within each pulse. Higher reads as a more urgent buzz.
How fast the buzz stutters. Faster feels like an aggressive soft-cut limiter.
How much of each pulse is filled with sound. Higher = more sustained; lower = more punctuated.

Cuts vibrations while the car is in the air, so a jump feels weightless. Works in Assetto Corsa, Forza, and Farming Simulator (with the TF4ALL Enhanced Telemetry mod), and does nothing in other games.
How far to turn the chosen effects down while airborne. 100% = fully silent; lower values just dial them back.

The wheel's steering force is built from telemetry instead of the game's own FFB. Works in Forza Motorsport (2023) and Forza Horizon 4, 5, and 6. Set the game's force feedback and vibration to 0 so this is the only force on the wheel. Farming Simulator 22 and 25 are supported too, through the spring option below.

The game is still sending its own force feedback, so two force streams are fighting and the wheel will feel jumpy or buzzy. In the game's wheel settings, set force feedback and vibration strength to 0 so this is the only force on the wheel.

Learns how hard each car pushes the wheel, then scales it to match your Strength setting.
Levels cars out so every car lands at the heaviness your Strength slider sets. The trade: cars stop feeling lighter or heavier than each other. Takes a few laps per car to settle.
Forget what this car has learned and start again. Use it after a tune or a tire change makes the wheel feel wrong. This also clears the car's learned grip calibration.

The smallest force your wheel actually plays here: lifts faint terrain hits, and light centering once the wheel is off dead-ahead, above the wheel's own friction. Raise it on a belt-driven wheel (G923) until faint bumps just move the wheel. A parked wheel stays limp, and damping is unaffected.

The peak steering force this car itself produces, in Nm. Not your wheel's rating: it is the car's number, scaled to fit inside your Strength setting. Lower it and this car leans harder on the wheel; raise it and this car feels lighter.

The peak steering force this car itself produces, in Nm. Not your wheel's rating: it is the car's number, scaled to fit inside your Strength setting. Lower it and this car leans harder on the wheel; raise it and this car feels lighter.

The force level this car peaks at, on a 0 to 1 scale. Lower it to make this car lean harder on the wheel; raise it to make it lighter. Apply fills it from what the plugin has watched this car push.

How strong the WHEEL should be. Your overall preference, roughly a percentage of the wheel's total power. It applies to every car; tune an individual car with its peak force instead.

Above this the strongest moments will clip: Auto leaves about 10 percent spare, and past that the top of big corners flattens off instead of building. Fine if you like it, but detail is lost where the car is working hardest.
The only force control you should need day to day. 1.00 delivers what the sim asked for. Raise it if the wheel feels light, lower it if it clips.
Resistance to wheel motion. The heavy, planted feel that is not grip force.
Smooths the force before it reaches the wheel. Higher = smoother feel but more lag; lower = tighter response. 0 = none, the default.
Smooths the force before it reaches the wheel. Higher = smoother feel but more lag; lower = tighter response. 0 = none, the default.
Leave smoothing at 0 unless the wheel feels notchy or grainy.

Softens the jolt of a curb strike and the buzz of a rumble strip, and leaves everything else alone. The sim reports each wheel's suspension speed six times a frame and says when the car is on a strip; the torque samples from those instants are eased toward the cornering load.
Eases the jolt of a curb strike and the buzz of a rumble strip. Off the curb, nothing changes.
How much of the strike is taken out. 0 leaves it as the sim sent it; 1 flattens it to the cornering load.
How much of the strike is taken out. 0 leaves it as the sim sent it; 1 flattens it to the cornering load.
How much of the strike is taken out. 0.60 keeps the hit but takes the sting off it.

Stops the wheel where the car's steering stops. The sim normally does this through its own force feedback, which is off while the plugin carries the force, so the plugin renders the stop itself from the sim's steering position and lock.
Stops the wheel where the car's steering stops.
How hard the stop pushes back, as a share of the wheel's full force. 1.00 is a wall; lower lets a determined push through.
How hard the stop pushes back, as a share of the wheel's full force. 1.00 is a wall; lower lets a determined push through.
How hard the stop pushes back. 1.00 is the wheel's full force.
On by default. Field texture, ruts, and edges reach the wheel as steering force, not just the spring's centering.
Bumps and ground texture reach the wheel as steering force. Needs the TF4ALL Enhanced Telemetry mod in the game (the plugin offers to install it).
How hard the ground hits back.
0 turns the spring off entirely, so you can feel what remains (terrain, damping, effects).
How solid the wheel feels right at center. Higher = crisper straight-line feel without heavier edges.
How much speed strengthens the centering. 0 = the same at every speed; 1 = fully speed-scaled with a limp standstill.

The steering grows heavier while your equipment is actually working the ground, a plow at depth pulls the wheel down, an empty run stays light. Plain engine strain (hard throttle, hills, hauling) adds a smaller touch of the same weight.
How much working equipment weighs the wheel.
How much of that weight plain engine strain applies with nothing working: hard throttle, hills, heavy hauling. 0 = implements only, 1 = strain counts in full.
The wheel loads up through turns based on how hard the vehicle is actually yawing. Most noticeable at road speeds.
How much cornering load weighs the wheel.
Follows the wheel's own position, so a released wheel settles into center instead of swinging past.
Caster-style pull toward straight, scaled up with speed (a parked wheel stays free).
How far ahead of the wheel's motion the centering aims. Raise if a released wheel overshoots center; lower if centering feels nervous.
Steering weight breathes with real front-axle load: braking dive loads up, crests go light.
Steering weight tops out just before the grip limit and holds, like a real tire; the plateau is your approach warning.
One front wheel hitting a bump or curb kicks the rim the way a real rack does; both wheels together cancel.
Torque left once the front has fully let go. Lower = a more dramatic gone-light cue.
Softens the wheel as you catch a slide back through center, so the moment the force switches sides stops snapping and feeling unstable. Digging deeper into a drift keeps its full weight.
A released wheel settles instead of oscillating, because the force is led slightly ahead of the wheel to cancel telemetry lag.
Raise the lead only until a released wheel stops ringing; too much adds nervousness on fast transitions.
Shapes both the grip limit and the braking fade to each car's measured grip as you brake or slide, instead of one fixed point. Off also restores the classic lockup fade.
The wheel lightens at each car's real grip limit, learned as you drive (about a lap of pushing). Off = a fixed manual grip limit (the slider below).
How quickly steering weight returns as the tires regain grip after a lockup or slide. Lower snaps back fast, higher hands the weight back gently.
Where the game's combined-slip metric counts as the grip limit (1.0 = Forza's own limit). Lower = the wheel peaks and washes out earlier.
Force shaping and plumbing. The defaults suit almost everyone.
How early weight arrives. Lower = heavier in normal cornering; 1.0 = force grows linearly to the limit.
Input smoothing. Higher = calmer wheel, slightly laggier response.
Soft ceiling on the steering force: stacked cornering weight and road kick compress into the top of the range instead of clipping flat.
Bases the steering force on cornering (lateral) grip instead of total grip.
Braking in a straight line makes almost no force, so the wheel cannot start swinging left and right on its own. Cornering feel is unchanged.
Flip this if the wheel pulls INTO the slide instead of countering it.
Invert FFB sign (uncheck if forces feel reversed)
Flips the direction of the game's force feedback sent to the wheel. On by default. If your wheel pushes the wrong way (e.g. forces feel reversed in RaceRoom), uncheck this.
Adds back the game's low-speed parking resistance, which the handed-over, Telemetry Based and Farming Simulator routes otherwise drop. Firm when parked, fading to nothing as you gain speed.
How firm the parked resistance is, as a share of full wheel force.
How firm the parked resistance is. Higher is heavier; too high can start to shake, so it tops out where it stays smooth.
The car speed at which the stationary friction has faded to nothing. Below it the friction eases off as you speed up; above it, only the sim's own force remains.
The car speed at which the stationary friction has faded to nothing.
Firm when parked, easing off as you gain speed and gone by this speed (km/h).

A parked car sends almost no force feedback, so the wheel feels limp. This adds a centering weight that fades out as you start moving and never fights the game's own FFB. It is set per game and off until you tick it, in Assetto Corsa, RaceRoom, Le Mans Ultimate or Forza with Telemetry Based FFB. Ignored for iRacing (the sim already weights the wheel).
Skipped in Forza, where it can fight the game's own force feedback around pauses and drag the wheel hard to one side. Your tuning still applies in other games.
How much centering weight to add when fully parked, as a fraction of full FFB. Start low; a strong spring can snap the wheel to center hard.
The spring is at full strength when stopped and fades to nothing by this speed. Keep it low so it's gone before real cornering forces build.
FFB spike reduction (recommended for Assetto Corsa)

Some games deliver curb and collision FFB spikes well beyond what's safe or comfortable on stronger wheelbases (Assetto Corsa is the worst offender we've seen). Hits can be sharp enough to wrench the wheel against your grip or strain your wrists on a long session.
The method picked below only applies while the box above is checked.

The most a hit may rise above that running average. However hard the game hits, that is where it levels off, so a curb strike mid-corner lands this much above the corner instead of wrenching the wheel.

Holds the running average up to at least this much, so ordinary force on a smooth road is not mistaken for a hit. It is also where a hit starts being slowed. Set it below normal road feel and everyday bumps start getting flattened and slowed.

iRacing sends telemetry 60 times a second, and each update carries six force samples from the physics steps in between. These options choose whether to fill the gaps between updates and how much of that extra detail to use.
How bright the wheel's lights are, for every pattern. This is the wheel's own setting and it stays where you put it.

Play an effect through the wheel's own firmware (native: the reference feel), then the same effect through the plugin's renderer, and tune until they match. The gain belongs to the picked effect, so you can tune one effect, switch to the next, and tune that one without disturbing the first. Native playback needs the wheel free (no game running). Save stores every effect's tuning as the default for future sessions.
The effect to compare. The gain below belongs to whichever effect is picked here, so each one tunes and saves separately.
The wheel's own DirectInput effect with the Trueforce stream fully STOPPED: the wheel exactly as it is without the plugin. The reference feel.
The identical effect through the plugin's renderer, streamed as Trueforce force: what games feel under the plugin.

Records every force tick to a CSV in Documents\TrueforceForAll: the wheel's velocity as the reader measures it, the smoothed velocity the damper actually multiplies, and the force each effect added. Play an effect, turn the wheel through whatever feels wrong, then press again to save. Keeps the last 30 seconds, so a long recording is fine.

Scales the picked effect only: each family (damper, spring, friction, inertia, waveforms, ramp) keeps its own gain, so you can tune one, switch, and tune the next. Live while an engine effect plays. Save tuning stores them all.
Puts the picked effect's gain back to its shipped default. The other effects keep their tuning.

On (default) is real inertia: the wheel resists the push, then carries on turning as the stored energy comes back. Off makes it only ever resist, which is what the wheel's own firmware does. Affects inertia only.

Off (default) renders inertia properly, from how fast the wheel is speeding up. On renders it from how fast the wheel is turning instead, which is how the wheel's own native inertia feels. For A/B against the firmware. The inertia gain means a different thing in each mode, so retune after switching.
Flips the velocity-coupled effects (damper, friction, inertia) if the rendered damper feels like an anti-damper. Springs never flip.

Low-pass on the PICKED condition's rendered output (anti-ringing). Per-effect, like the gain: each condition (damper, spring, friction, inertia) keeps its own, so drop the damper's below ~70 Hz to smooth a grainy damper without touching the rest. Follows the shared filter until you move it; Save tuning keeps it. 0 = off. Waveforms have no condition filter (greyed).

Run the calibration five times from the SAME starting gains and take the median, reporting the spread. More samples tighten the median: the noisier a measurement is, the more it needs them. Successive single runs are not independent (each measures a correction relative to the gains it starts from), so this is the way to tell a repeatable measurement from a noisy one. Takes about five times as long.

Hands-free calibration (about a minute, hands OFF the wheel): bounded self-pulses measure the wheel's native damper, spring and friction against the plugin's renderer and set the gains to match; also measures the real native-vs-stream force scale. Verify by feel afterwards, then Save. Stop cancels.
Persists every effect's gain plus direction and filter as the defaults for every session (auto-tune and DAMPCAL update gains too; save afterwards to keep them).
Puts every effect's gain, the direction and the filter back to shipped defaults. Live only: Save afterwards to keep it, or reopen SimHub to get your saved tuning back.

Most setups receive fine on 127.0.0.1. If you're getting zero packets, work through these:
• Confirm Forza's DATA OUT is ON, and its IP and PORT match this plugin (IP 127.0.0.1, PORT = the Port field above).
• Port collision with SimHub or another tool? Pick a different port here, then update Forza's DATA OUT IP PORT to match.

• Still nothing on 127.0.0.1: set Forza's DATA OUT IP ADDRESS to your PC's LAN IP (e.g. 192.168.x.x) instead, and leave the bind address here at 0.0.0.0. This gets around localhost quirks on some installs.
• Firewall: Windows Defender may prompt the first time the listener opens. Allow it on private/domain networks.

Smaller ring buffers = less latency between game and wheel, but require Windows to wake our threads on time.

Drop both rings back to the smallest configured value. In Auto mode the ratchet will re-discover whether your machine can hold them.
Sample buffer between the audio mixer and the USB stream. Smaller = lower wheel latency, but Windows must wake the stream thread on time.

Sample buffer between WASAPI loopback and the audio mixer. Runs 16 to 128 samples; 16 is both the smallest and the default. If you hear continuous clicks, raise it, or let the auto-ratchet (Auto mode) raise it for you.

Counters tally events in a rolling 60-second window. If they are going up, your machine is glitching at the current ring size.
